paper.title: Fluid Antennas Enabled UAV Communication Systems: Fundamentals, Challenges, and Future Directions
paper.abstract: Low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) require uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) communication systems to adapt to large-scale propagation changes and fast local channel fluctuations. Fluid antennas (FAs) provide an additional degree of freedom (DoF) by reconfiguring antenna positions within a compact aperture. This article investigates FA-enabled UAV communication systems from the perspectives of fundamentals, design challenges, and future research directions. We first introduce a dual-mobility perspective, in which UAV trajectory planning provides macro-mobility for large-scale air-to-ground geometry adaptation, and FA position reconfiguration provides micro-mobility for fine-grained local channel adaptation. We then identify key design challenges arising from the high computational complexity and information uncertainty in the joint optimization of UAV trajectory, FA positions, and beamforming under mobility, energy, hardware, and security constraints. To address these challenges, we present a hybrid offline-online optimization framework, where prior information such as environment maps, user mobility patterns, and statistical channel state information (CSI) supports long-term planning, while real-time information such as instantaneous CSI and UAV state enables fast online correction. A case study on FA-enabled UAV-assisted vehicular communications demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Finally, we discuss future directions of FA-enabled UAV communication in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), secure communication, mobile edge computing (MEC), and aerial relaying.

paper.title: Radiomics-Based Thyroid Nodule Classification with Label-Conditional Conformal Prediction
paper.abstract: Thyroid nodule malignancy assessment relies on ultrasound imaging, yet current risk stratification systems suffer from substantial interobserver variability, contributing to a high rate of unnecessary biopsies. We propose a radiomics-based framework combining quantitative feature extraction via PyRadiomics with a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) classifier, selected among six candidates for its favorable trade-off between discriminative performance and interpretability. To complement point predictions with uncertainty estimates, Cross-Conformal Prediction with label-conditional guarantees is applied, flagging ambiguous cases for clinical review rather than forcing a binary decision. Experiments are conducted on TN5000, a publicly available ultrasound dataset of thyroid nodules. After Spearman correlation filtering, 36 features are retained and the GAM achieves an AUC of $0.89$, a sensitivity of $0.83$, and a specificity of $0.82$ on the validation set. At a significance level $ε=0.09$, selected to ensure empirical coverage guarantees on both classes, 63\% of nodules on the test set receive a certain (i.e., single-label) prediction, with conditional precision of $0.94$ for certain malignant and conditional Negative Predictive Value (NPV) of $0.73$ for certain benign cases, while the remaining 37\% are referred to the clinician.

paper.title: How well do routinely collected demographic and clinical variables aid point-of-care lung ultrasound TB classification
paper.abstract: We consider the fusion of lung ultrasound images with routinely-collected clinical and demographic data for the purpose of automated tuberculosis (TB) screening using deep-learning. Such deep-learning based screening tools for TB could meaningfully support the health care system in Africa, where the burden of disease is severe and resources are constrained. Beginning with an established ResNet baseline for classification of lung ultrasound images, which achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve of 0.91 [0.86,0.96] (95% CI), we consider the incorporation of the clinical and demographic data using three fusion approaches. We find that a simple average-based fusion of the output scores of separately-trained image and clinical data classifiers consistently matches or outperforms a more complex approach where the data is fused earlier and a combined classifier is trained. Fusing the image and the clinical classifiers in this way leads to a classifier with an overall AUROC of 0.95 [0.91,0.99] (specificity of 0.76 at sensitivity 0.93) which is an improvement of 4% absolute over the image-only baseline. We also find that greedy feature selection can be used to reduce the number of clinical and demographic inputs without sacrificing classification performance. Finally, when we differentiate between clinical and demographic data that are self-reported, that require some basic measurement or calculation, and that require a point-of-care (POC) test, we find the inclusion of the POC tests included in this study to be of minimal benefit to classification performance. We conclude that the incorporation of routinely-collected clinical and demographic data is a promising way to improve the performance of lung ultrasound based automatic classification.

paper.title: Learning to Measure and Diagnose: A Clinical-Dictionary Radiomic Bottleneck Model for Thyroid Nodule Classification
paper.abstract: Thyroid ultrasound supports the assessment of nodule malignancy, but classification predictions often lack evidence linked to familiar clinical descriptions. Radiomics provides explicitly defined measurements that can support such explanations through a clinical dictionary. However, using these measurements as interpretable evidence requires reliable estimation from ultrasound images and preservation of measurement fidelity when optimizing classification performance. We propose a clinical-dictionary radiomic bottleneck model for thyroid nodule classification. Within this model, Family-Aware Radiomic Learning (FARL) estimates measurements with balanced supervision across feature families. Fidelity-Guided Bottleneck Modeling (FGBM) constructs a fixed bottleneck, followed by joint optimization of measurement estimation and classification under fidelity guidance. Decision evidence decomposition then traces feature contributions through a linear classifier and organizes them by clinical dictionary categories. Experiments on ThyroidXL and TN3K show competitive classification performance, while case studies illustrate feature contributions for benign and malignant nodules. These findings indicate interpretable classification with inspectable quantitative evidence informed by clinical knowledge. Code is available online.

paper.title: Variational Bayesian Inference Based Progressive Multi-Target MIMO Sensing with Nuisance Parameters
paper.abstract: This paper proposes a progressive Bayesian multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) sensing framework for multiple targets over multiple stages. We consider a practical yet challenging scenario where the targets' angles are unknown and random parameters to be estimated, while the targets' reflection coefficients are unknown nuisance parameters. With an initial prior probability density function (PDF) for the targets' angles, we progressively update the prior PDF for each sensing stage as the posterior PDF obtained from the previous stage, based on which Bayesian transmit beamforming optimization is performed to minimize the sum posterior Cramér-Rao bound (PCRB) in estimating the targets' angles and Bayesian sensing is performed with the help of new observations in this stage. To analytically characterize the intractable and high-dimensional posterior PDF with low complexity, we propose a variational Bayesian inference based approach which derives a surrogate posterior PDF in closed form with only polynomial complexity over the number of targets, in sharp contrast to existing numerical calculation approaches with exponential complexity. Numerical results validate the efficacy of our proposed framework in progressively refining sensing performance.

paper.title: On the Performance of Randomly Generated Codebooks in Near-Field Communications
paper.abstract: Near-field communication with large antenna arrays requires beamforming techniques that account for spherical wavefront effects. While predefined codebooks are widely used in multiple-antenna wireless systems, the performance of randomly generated codebooks in the near-field region has not been investigated. In this work, we study four randomly generated codebooks for near-field communications: random vector quantization (RVQ), random phase (RP), random far-field (RFF), and random near-field (RNF) codebooks. We use the known RVQ gain distribution as a benchmark. For RP, we derive a large-array bulk approximation and characterize the high-gain tail behavior of the gain distribution. For RNF, we characterize the high-gain tail behavior of the gain distribution. For RFF, we derive an analytical approximation for the maximum achievable beamforming gain when far-field beams are used to serve near-field users, along with the corresponding maximizing far-field direction. We also analyze the maximum-gain scaling with codebook size. Monte Carlo simulations verify the analytical results and show that RVQ and RP degrade significantly as the array size increases, while RNF achieves the most favorable high-gain scaling. RFF can outperform RVQ and RP for finite codebook sizes, but its maximum gain saturates below one due to the phase mismatch between the far-field beams and the near-field channel. These results show how codebook structure, array size, and codebook size affect random beamforming performance in the near-field.

paper.title: Movable-Element Multi-Functional RIS-Assisted Hybrid RSMA-NOMA: A Constrained Hybrid Reinforcement Learning Approach
paper.abstract: In this work, we propose a movable-element (ME) multi-functional reconfigurable intelligent surface (MF-RIS) architecture, termed MM-RIS, which integrates element mobility with adaptive signal reflection, transmission, amplification, and energy harvesting (EH) to enhance communication flexibility and energy self-sustainability. A hybrid rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) transmission scheme is further designed to improve spectral efficiency. We formulate an energy efficiency (EE) maximization problem by jointly optimizing transmit beamforming, power and rate allocation, MM-RIS configurations, panel deployment, and ME positions. To address the resulting non-convex mixed continuous-discrete optimization problem, we propose constrained hybrid deep reinforcement learning with federated transformer and parametrized sharing (CRAFTS). CRAFTS integrates multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) and multi-agent deep Q-networks (MADQN) through bi-directional parametrized sharing to handle continuous and discrete actions, respectively. Moreover, a transformer-based architecture and federated learning (FL) are incorporated to enhance state representation and distributed knowledge sharing, whilst a Lagrangian-based adaptive penalty mechanism facilitates the constraint satisfaction. Simulation results have demonstrated that the proposed MM-RIS architecture and CRAFTS framework substantially improve EE and constraint satisfaction compared to the benchmarks in the open literature. Moreover, the results validate the benefits of spatially reconfigurable MM-RIS, hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions, and intelligent collaborative learning, highlighting the potential of the proposed framework for energy-efficient and adaptive next-generation wireless networks.

\begin{abstract}
In this work, we propose a movable-element (ME) multi-functional reconfigurable intelligent surface (MF-RIS) architecture, termed MM-RIS, which integrates element mobility with adaptive signal reflection, transmission, amplification, and energy harvesting (EH) to enhance communication flexibility and energy self-sustainability. CRAFTS integrates multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) and multi-agent deep Q-networks (MADQN) through bi-directional parametrized sharing to handle continuous and discrete actions, respectively. Moreover, a transformer-based architecture and federated learning (FL) are incorporated to enhance state representation and distributed knowledge sharing, whilst a Lagrangian-based adaptive penalty mechanism facilitates the constraint satisfaction. Simulation results have demonstrated that the proposed MM-RIS architecture and CRAFTS framework substantially improve EE and constraint satisfaction compared to the benchmarks in the open literature. Moreover, the results validate the benefits of spatially reconfigurable MM-RIS, hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions, and intelligent collaborative learning, highlighting the potential of the proposed framework for energy-efficient and adaptive next-generation wireless networks.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\subsection{Background and Literature Reviews}
In the era of sixth-generation (6G) wireless communications, the scarcity of spectrum resources and the explosive growth in heterogeneous service demands have driven researchers to explore more efficient and flexible transmission technologies \cite{1}. To further enhance spectral and interference management in dense wireless deployments, rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) has recently emerged as a highly promising transmission strategy \cite{2}. By splitting messages into common and private components and superimposing them through linear precoding, RSMA provides flexible interference handling. Owing to this flexibility, RSMA demonstrates improved robustness against imperfect channel state information and offers superior rate-reliability trade-offs in interference-limited environments \cite{3}. However, despite its advantages, the performance of RSMA may still be insufficient in highly dynamic or heavily loaded networks, where interference suppression remains challenging. To further maximize its performance potential, successive interference cancellation (SIC) from non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) \cite{noma} can be incorporated into RSMA, forming a hybrid structure. By combining rate-splitting capability of RSMA with power-domain multiplexing of NOMA \cite{7}, such hybrid design enhances multi-user signal separation and strengthens interference mitigation, enabling greater spectral efficiency and improved link reliability. However, the performance of such multiple accesses is often hindered by severe channel fading and inter-user interference, which potentially degrades the signal quality and limits its practical deployment \cite{9}. 
To address the above-mentioned issues, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) have been proposed as an enabling technology \cite{10, 11}. By adjusting the configuration of RIS elements, a virtual line-of-sight (LoS) link can be established to bypass obstacles between the transmitter and receiver and to improve the signal quality for combating the channel fading \cite{my_fdris3, 12}. Benefited from these advantages, RIS can enable precise signal distribution, significantly improving communication performances. Although RIS holds promise for next-generation wireless networks, its practical deployment remains constrained by several inherent limitations. Specifically, it can only be operated over a 180-degree half-space coverage area, and mainly depends on external power supplies, which confines its independent operation and scalability. To overcome the backdrops, the concept of multi-functional RIS (MF-RIS) has been introduced in \cite{14, my_ojcom}, integrating simultaneous transmission and reflection (STAR) capabilities to provide 360-degree full-space coverage and ubiquitous connectivity \cite{15, 16, my_star}. Additionally, MF-RIS is equipped with radio-frequency (RF) and energy harvesting (EH) circuits, enabling it to capture energy from incident electromagnetic signals and is capable of operating in a self-sustainable manner \cite{18, 19, 20}. Such design alleviates the dependence on wired power infrastructure or frequent battery replacement, enhancing the overall energy efficiency (EE). Furthermore, by embedding active components, MF-RIS is capable of conducting signal amplification \cite{22} for compensating severe path loss, improving the quality-of-services (QoS) of users in weak channel conditions. When combined with advanced multiple access schemes, MF-RIS can substantially strengthen the propagation conditions for user clusters, especially under NOMA-/RSMA-based transmissions. 
However, the practical implementation of active MF-RIS is also hindered by hardware-induced constraints such as the coupled phase-shift effects \cite{23}. Unlike ideal models, active components frequently exhibit a strong interdependence between the phase-shift and amplification gains \cite{24}. This coupling effect might reduce the available DoFs in the optimization space, which necessitates more complex coordination strategies to achieve the desired beamforming gains. To overcome these limitations, beyond static metasurfaces, fluid antenna (FA) systems have recently attracted attention for their ability to dynamically reconfigure the effective antenna position within a given aperture by leveraging fluid-based elements \cite{my_lim, 26}. Similar to FA, movable-antenna (MA) structures \cite{MA1, new1, new2, new3, new4} are also developed. By allowing the radiating point to move within a predefined region, FA/MA can exploit spatial diversity in small-scale fading without requiring multiple RF chains, offering new degrees of freedom (DoFs) at the physical layer. This dynamic ability is particularly appealing in environments with rapidly varying channels or strong blockage effects. In the works of \cite{new1, new2}, antenna position of the MA is deployed to increase the spatial DoF and enhance the performance of the integrated sensing and communication systems. The paper \cite{new3} investigates that the MA is capable of achieving full array gain over the desired direction, whereas null steering in undesired directions can be realized. The work of \cite{new4} further discusses near-field digital and analog beamforming in MA-aided multiuser communication systems. In the work of \cite{6dma}, six-dimensional MA is introduced that exploits the transceiver spatial variation by considering both xyz-positions and rotations to improve performance in terms of geometric array gains, spatial multiplexing and interference mitigation. Inspired by the FA/MA \cite{fas1, 10, MA1, new1, new2, new3, new4}, the movable-elements (ME) are introduced \cite{25, lim1, pat, movele1} to enable element-wise spatial adjustment across three-dimensional (3D) Cartesian axes of xyz-domain. Different from MAs, ME-enhanced RIS further aligning to proper small-scale channels induces a more challenging task when configuring well-positioned elements in the cascaded channels from the base station (BS), RIS to users \cite{lim1}. The authors in \cite{26} have proposed a movable-element RIS (ME-RIS) framework, utilizing an element-wise position optimization approach to significantly enhance beamforming gains. Furthermore, the concept of fluid-element STAR surfaces called FIRES is designed in \cite{27}, which extends the FA capability to STAR-RIS architectures. In paper \cite{new5}, MA-aided NOMA is considered for multi-user downlink communications, where the MA positions at the users, BS beamforming, and SIC decoding indicators are jointly optimized. Moreover, the work of \cite{new6} investigates the benefits of FA with dynamic port reconfiguration for enhancing RSMA performance, where the outage probability and ergodic rate are analyzed to quantify the performance gains provided by FA. However, most existing FA/MA-integrated works focus on single-link scenarios or basic reflection/transmission structures, relying on the external power grid usage. The integration of ME into MF-RISs that simultaneously supports element mobility, reflection/transmission capability, signal amplification, and self-sustainable EH remains largely unexplored. 
With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), the integration of learning-based optimizations into wireless communication systems has become an important research trend \cite{11, 29}, especially for complex environments. Owing to the strong coupling between multiple strategies such as beamforming and RIS configurations, the resulting optimization problems typically exhibit high dimensionality, non-linearity, and mixed discrete-continuous structures, rendering traditional analytical or convex-approximation methods inadequate in highly dynamic environments. In addressing these challenges, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been widely adopted for resource allocation and control \cite{11, my_rl_wu, 30, han, 31, my_rl_yt} thanks to its capability of learning near-optimal policies from interactions with complex environments. In DRL, an agent performs the determined actions and then attains rewards, followed by the observed updated states for the next-round policy decision. In \cite{11}, a multi-agent system is considered, where each agent corresponds to an individual RIS, and the joint beamforming and RIS deployment are optimized using multi-agent RL techniques. In paper \cite{29}, a multi-agent system is designed for low-complexity beamforming and power control in multi-antenna-based NOMA networks. The work of \cite{my_rl_wu} designs a hierarchical RL structure for RIS optimizations, where the core-RL optimizes the beamforming and configurations, whereas auxiliary RL optimizes the hyperparameters of core-RL for better learning process. Nonetheless, most existing DRL approaches are either centralized, leading to scalability and overhead issues, or designed for purely continuous or purely discrete state-action spaces, which are inadequate for complex wireless networks. This motivates the development of hybrid DRL frameworks that can handle continuous-discrete action spaces in a unified manner \cite{30, han, 31, my_ojcom}. In the work of \cite{30}, hybrid continuous and discrete action outputs are designed as a parametrized sharing architecture. Extended from \cite{30}, the paper \cite{han} designs hybrid DRL for tackling continuous STAR-RIS configurations and the discrete coupled-phase problems. The work of \cite{31} designs twin-models and bi-directional sharing structure in hybrid DRL architecture for complex MF-RIS policies associated with continuous-discrete actions. 
Furthermore, conventional DRL architectures relying solely on multiple deep neural layer learning may struggle to capture complex dependencies between high-dimensional states and actions, especially in multi-agent coordination. To address this, adoption of transformer architectures \cite{32, my_ojcom} for enhancing feature extraction and representation learning is needed \cite{my_ojcom, 33}. Additionally, federated learning (FL) \cite{34} is utilized for enabling decentralized model aggregation and privacy-aware knowledge sharing across distributed learning agents without raw data exchange. In addition to architectural enhancements, ensuring strict adherence to operational boundaries such as QoS and power limits is crucial for practical reliability. While conventional reward shaping is often used to penalize constraint violations, its static nature frequently fails to maintain an optimal balance between performance optimization and safety requirements \cite{35, 37}. This necessitates the adoption of Lagrangian-based primal-dual optimization techniques \cite{35}, i.e., an adaptive Lagrangian multiplier method to dynamically tune penalty coefficients based on instantaneous violations. However, the applications of enhanced architectures of multi-agent hybrid DRL with transformer, parametrized sharing, federated cooperation, and adaptive Lagrangian constraint management to complex wireless network systems remain substantially unexplored. \subsection{Challenges and Contributions}
The integration of ME and MF-RIS with hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions remains unstudied but introduces several fundamental challenges. The incorporation of MEs into MF-RIS significantly enlarges the spatial DoFs, leading to a high-dimensional and highly-coupled optimization problem involving beamforming, power control, rate allocation, phase-shift coefficients, and metasurface locations as well as element positions. The comparable overhead associated with ME, including movement power consumption and repositioning delay may be introduced and cannot be neglected compared to the operational power and channel coherence time. This results in a non-convex mixed continuous-discrete problem that is difficult to solve using conventional optimization techniques. Additionally, the hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmission scheme introduces complex interference structures across clustered users, which require dynamic and coordinated resource allocation to strike a compelling balance between spectral efficiency and interference mitigation. The coupling transmissions among communication variables further increases the difficulty of joint optimization. Furthermore, the presence of EH and amplification functionalities imposes stringent system constraints of power budgets, QoS requirements, and hardware limitations. Self-sustainable capability should be achieved while supporting multiple functionalities of MF-RIS. From algorithmic perspectives, the large-scale multi-agent nature of complex wireless networks leads to scalability and non-stationarity issues, where centralized learning becomes impractical due to excessive overhead, whilst decentralized learning suffers from limited coordination and potential convergence issues. This motivates us to conceive an advanced DRL-based framework for the integration of ME and MF-RIS in hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions. The main contributions of this paper are elaborated as follows:
\begin{itemize}
	\item We propose a novel ME-enhanced MF-RIS (MM-RIS)-assisted communication framework for hybrid RSMA-NOMA downlink transmissions. The proposed MM-RIS integrates MEs with a deployable MF-RIS capabilities, enabling adaptive signal reflection, transmission, amplification, and EH, which significantly enhances system adaptability, coverage, and energy self-sustainability in dynamic wireless environments.
	\item We formulate an EE maximization problem for the proposed MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA. The problem jointly optimizes transmit beamforming, power and rate allocation, MM-RIS parameters of amplitude coefficients, phase-shifts, and EH ratios, as well as metasurface deployment and ME positions. The formulated problem is highly non-convex and involves mixed continuous-discrete variables with intricate coupling constraints under practical limitations such as BS power budgets, user rate requirements and rate allocation bounds as well as minimum inter-element spacing, coupled phase-shifts, self-sustainability, and deployment boundaries of MM-RIS.
	\item We develop a constrained hybrid reinforcement learning framework with federated transformer and parametrized sharing (CRAFTS) scheme which integrates multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) and multi-agent deep Q-network (MADQN) to handle continuous and discrete decision variables, respectively. A transformer-based architecture is incorporated to capture complex state-action dependencies, while FL is employed to facilitate decentralized training and accelerate convergence via collaborative knowledge sharing. Moreover, a bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanism is proposed to enable coordinated optimization across heterogeneous action spaces. Furthermore, to guarantee constraint satisfaction, a Lagrangian-based adaptive penalty mechanism is conceived to dynamically update multipliers, ensuring stable and reliable learning under practical system constraints.
	\item Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed CRAFTS-enabled MM-RIS framework significantly outperforms the conventional benchmarks, including standalone PPO/DQN, non-coupled learning benchmarks, and different single-functional RIS architectures without amplification or EH in the open literature. Particularly, the proposed MM-RIS-aided RSMA-NOMA achieves substantial EE gains and constraint satisfaction across diverse scenarios, validating the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed architecture for next-generation wireless networks.

\subsection{Channel Model}
We consider the Rician fading channel model \cite{31} between the BS and the $q$-th MM-RIS as $\mathbf{H}_{q} \in \mathbb{C}^{M \times N}$
\begin{align}
	\mathbf{H}_q = \sqrt{h_0 d_{q}^{-k_0}}
\left( \sqrt{\frac{\beta_0}{\beta_0 + 1}} \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{\beta_0 + 1}} \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}} \right),
\label{4}
\end{align}
where $h_0$ is the pathloss at the reference distance of 1 meter, $d_{q}= \|\mathbf{w}_b-\mathbf{w}_q\| $ is the distance between BS and MM-RIS $q$, and $k_0$ is the pathloss exponent. Notation of $\beta_0$ represents the Rician factor adjusting the portion of LoS path $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}}$ and non-LoS (NLoS) component of $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}}$. The LoS component $ \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} $ is expressed as \cite{26} $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} = \mathbf{a}'_q(\psi'_{a,q}, \psi'_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q) \mathbf{a}_b^{\mathrm{H}}(\psi_b)$,
where $(\cdot)^{\mathrm{H}}$ indicates the Hermitian operation. The transmit steering vector of the BS and the receiving steering vector of the $q$-th MM-RIS associated with the $m$-th ME are respectively given by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align}
	[\mathbf{a}_b(\psi_b)]_n &= e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} (n-1) \sin(\psi_b)}, 
	[\mathbf{a}_q(\psi'_{a,q}, \psi'_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)]_m  &= e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left(x_{q,m} \sin\psi'_{a,q} \cos\psi'_{e,q} + y_{q,m} \sin\psi'_{e,q}\right)},
 \label{6}
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $[ \cdot ]_n$ represents the $n$-th entry of the vector. Notation of $\lambda$ indicates the wavelength, whilst $\psi_b$ denotes the angle-of-departure (AoD) from the BS towards MM-RIS. Symbols of $\psi'_{a,q}$ and $\psi'_{e,q}$ denote the azimuth and elevation angles-of-arrival (AoAs) at MM-RIS $q$, respectively. Following \eqref{4}, the channel between the $q$-th MM-RIS and user $U_{kj}$ is defined as $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj} \in \mathbb{C}^{M\times 1}$, where the distance between them is denoted as $d_{q, kj} = \| \mathbf{w}_q - \mathbf{w}_{kj} \|$. The LoS channel of $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}$ can be expressed as $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{LoS}} = \mathbf{a}''_q (\psi''_{a,q}, \psi''_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)$,
where $\psi''_{a,q}$ and $\psi''_{e,q}$ respectively denote the azimuth and elevation AoDs from the MM-RIS towards user $U_{kj}$, and the corresponding elementwise steering vector is defined as
\begin{align}
 [\mathbf{a}''_q (\psi''_{a,q}, \psi''_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)]_m  = e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left(x_{q,m} \sin\psi''_{a,q} \cos\psi''_{e,q} + y_{q,m} \sin\psi''_{e,q}\right)}.
 \label{eq:fires_user_channel}
\end{align}
As for the NLoS components related to MM-RIS-based channel, i.e., $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{NLoS}}$, Jake's model is adopted to model the ME-induced spatial correlation \cite{my_lim}, i.e., $[\mathbf{J}_{q}]_{i,j} = J_0 \left( \frac{2\pi \Delta d_{i,j}}{\lambda} \right)$, where $J_0$ is the Bessel function of the zero order and $\Delta d_{i,j}$ denotes the distances between the $i$-th and the $j$-th MM-RIS elements. The spatial correlation can be further written as $\mathbf{J}_{q}= \mathbf{U}_q \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_q \mathbf{U}_q^{\mathrm{H}}$, where $\mathbf{U}_q$ is the unitary matrix with eigenvectors and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_q$ indicates the diagonal eigenvalue matrix. Accordingly, the expressions of the NLoS channels of $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}}$ and of $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{NLoS}}$ can be respectively derived by $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_q^{1/2} \mathbf{U}_q^{\mathrm{H}} \bar{\mathbf{H}}_q$ 
and
$\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{NLoS}} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_{q,kj}^{1/2} \mathbf{U}_{q,kj}^{\mathrm{H}} \bar{\mathbf{g}}_{q,kj}$
where $\bar{\mathbf{H}}_q$ and $\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{q,kj}$ represent the uncorrelated small-scale fading components, which are modeled as complex Gaussian distribution with zero mean and unit variance. The direct link from the BS to user $j$ at direction $k$ is denoted by $\mathbf{h}_{kj} \in \mathbb{C}^{N \times1 }$, associated with their distance of $d_{kj}$. While, the pertinent parameters of $\mathbf{h}_{kj}$ follow \eqref{4} but in a vector form, where the LoS component $ \mathbf{h}_{kj}^{\text{LoS}}$ is expressed as $\mathbf{h}^{\text{LoS}}_{kj} = \left[
1, e^{j\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}d_B\sin\varphi_{b}}, \ldots, e^{j\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}(N-1)d_B\sin\varphi_{b} } \right]^{\mathrm{T}}$, where $d_B$ denotes the element separation of BS. Notation of $\varphi_{b}$ represents the AoD of the BS towards user $U_{kj}$. Note that the NLoS part is defined as $\mathbf{h}^{\text{NLoS}}_{kj}$ following the Rayleigh fading. Consequently, the effective channel between the BS and user $U_{kj}$ is denoted as ${\mathbf{g}}_{kj} = \mathbf{h}_{kj}^{\mathrm{H}} + \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}} \mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\mathrm{H}} \mathbf{\Theta}_{q}^k \mathbf{H}_{q}$.
\subsection{Signal Model}
In the hybrid RSMA-NOMA downlink transmission, users are first partitioned into multiple groups to efficiently share the limited spectrum resources. Specifically, a channel-aware user grouping procedure is performed prior to resource optimization. Users are first classified according to whether they are located on the reflection or transmission side of the MM-RIS. Users on each side are then further partitioned into multiple groups according to their effective channel directions. For users $u$ and $v$, their channel correlation is defined as $\rho_{u,v} = \frac{ |\mathbf g_u\mathbf g_v^{\rm H}| }{ \|\mathbf g_u\|_2\|\mathbf g_v\|_2 }$. Users exhibiting high channel correlation are preferentially assigned to the same group to facilitate beamforming. In each group at direction $k$, data stream is split into common and private streams. The common stream decodes messages for all users, whereas the private stream provides individual data content to each user. Moreover, in private message, NOMA mechanism is employed to further superimpose private signals for enhancing the frequency utilizations. Therefore, the BS transmits signals containing the common stream $s_k^c$ and the private stream $s_{kj}$ for user $U_{kj}$. The signal received by user $U_{kj}$ can be given by

\begin{align} \label{r_signal}
& y_{kj} = 
	\underbrace{\mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_k^c \sqrt{p_{k}^c} s_{k}^c }_{\text{Common Stream}}
	+ \underbrace{\sum_{l\in\mathcal{K} \backslash k } \mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_{l}^c \sqrt{p_{l}^c} s_{l}^c }_{\text{Common Interf.}} 
	+ \underbrace{\mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_k^p \sqrt{p_{kj}} s_{kj}}_{\text{Private Stream}} \notag 
	& + \underbrace{\mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_k^p \sum_{i \in \mathcal{J}_k \setminus j} \sqrt{p_{ki}} s_{ki}}_{\text{Private Interf.}}
	+ \underbrace{\sum_{l \in \mathcal{K} \setminus k }\mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_{l}^p
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{J}_{l}} \sqrt{p_{li}} s_{li} }_{\text{Inter-Group Interf.}} \notag
	& + \underbrace{\sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}} \mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{H}}_{q,kj}\mathbf{\Theta}_{q}^k \mathbf{n}_q}_{\text{MM-RIS-Induced Noise}} + \underbrace{{n}_{kj}}_{\text{Background Noise}}, 
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $\mathbf{f}_k^c$ and $\mathbf{f}_k^p$ represent the transmit beamforming vectors for common and private streams of the BS at direction 
$k$, respectively, satisfying the power constraint of $\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \left( \|\mathbf{f}_k^c\|^2  + \|\mathbf{f}_k^p\|^2 \right) \leq P_{\text{BS}}^{\text{max}}$, where $P_{\text{BS}}^{\text{max}}$ denotes the transmit power budge of the BS. Moreover, $p_{k}^c$ and $p_{kj}$ are defined as the power allocation factor of common message at direction $k$ and that of private messages for user $U_{kj}$, whereas $p_{k}^c+\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} p_{kj} = 1$. Notation of $\mathbf{n}_{q} \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma_s^2 \mathbf{I}_M)$ denotes the amplification noise induced by the MM-RIS associated with its element noise power $\sigma_s^2$. Notation of $n_{kj}$ is background noise power of user $U_{kj}$, where its power is denoted as $\sigma_{u}^2$. Note that $\mathbf{f}_k^p$ is a group-level private precoder shared by all users within group $k$. Specifically, users with highly correlated effective channel directions are assigned to the same group and spatially served by $\mathbf f_k^p$, whereas their private messages are superimposed in the power domain using the user-specific power coefficients $p_{kj}$. Compared to assigning an independent precoder to every user, this group level design reduces the number of beamforming variables while retaining user differentiation through power-domain multiplexing.

To guarantee successful SIC, each stronger user decoding the message of $U_{kj}$ is required to achieve an SINR no smaller than that achieved by the intended user, i.e.,
\begin{align}

\geq

\quad
\forall l\in\mathcal{L}_{kj}\setminus j, j\in\mathcal{J}_k, k\in\mathcal{K},
\label{con_SIC}
\end{align}
where $\mathcal{L}_{kj} = \{j,j+1,...,J_k\}$. Accordingly, the SINR for user $U_{kj}$ to decode its own private message is obtained as the special case of $l=j$, i.e., $\gamma_{kj}^{p} = \gamma_{kj\rightarrow kj}^{p}$. Therefore, the achievable achievable private rate for $U_{kj}$ is given by $R_{kj}^p = \log_2(  1 + \gamma_{kj}^p)$. To ensure that all users can successfully decode the common data stream, the minimum achievable rate for decoding the common stream among all users must exceed the sum of the allocated common rates, which is expressed as $\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} R_{kj}^c \leq \min_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} C_{kj}$. Given the allocated common message rate $R_{kj}^c$ and achievable private message rate $R_{kj}^p$, the total rate of user $U_{kj}$ in hybrid RSMA-NOMA is represented by $r_{kj} = R_{kj}^c+R_{kj}^p$. During the repositioning of the MEs, the channel undergoes rapid time-varying fluctuations, potentially resulting in severe degradation of the received signal quality. Performing data transmission during this interval may therefore significantly impair the system performance. To mitigate this issue, we assume that only control signaling is retained between the BS and all users, whereas data transmission is temporarily halted during the ME movement phase. Accordingly, each transmission block of duration $T$ is partitioned into two phases, namely the ME movement phase and the communication phase. The effective sum rate of user $U_{kj}$ can be derived by \cite{27}
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{eff_rate}
	R_{kj} = \left(1-\frac{T_{\text{mov}}}{T} \right) \cdot r_{kj},
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $T_{\text{mov}}= \max_{q \in \mathcal{Q}, m\in \mathcal{M}}  \frac{\| \mathbf{r}_{q,m} - \mathbf{r}_{q,m}^0 \|}{v_{q,m}}$ represents the worst-case consumed time corresponding to the maximum moving distance among the MEs. It is worth noticing that the term $\left(1-\frac{T_{\text{mov}}}{T} \right)$ in \eqref{eff_rate} implies the ratio of the remaining time for data transmissions. Notations of $\mathbf{r}_{q,m}^0$ and $\mathbf{r}_{q,m}$ are the element position before and after the movement for the $m$-th element of the $q$-th MM-RIS. Note that $v_{q,m}$ indicates the velocity of each ME $m$. Note that the MM-RIS panel deployment and element-level ME repositioning are considered to operate on different timescales. Specifically, the MM-RIS panel positions are slow-timescale variables that are updated according to relatively slowly varying network conditions, such as user spatial distributions and large scale channel characteristics. In contrast, the MEs are locally repositioned within the surface region on a comparatively faster timescale to adapt to spatial channel variations. Accordingly, the movement-overhead term in the considered EE model accounts for the element-level ME reconfiguration, whereas the transient movement energy and delay associated with relocating an entire MM-RIS panel are not included in each communication optimization cycle.
To elaborate a little further, the proposed MM-RIS architecture can be extended to a general MIMO scenario where each user is equipped with multiple receive antennas. In this case, the equivalent effective channel between the BS and users will be generalized to a matrix-based channel, and additional receive beamforming should be introduced at users. Accordingly, the received signal and SINR can be reformulated by incorporating the receive beamforming, whilst the MM-RIS configurations remain applicable. The corresponding receive beamforming variables can be incorporated into the continuous action space of the proposed learning framework.
\subsection{EH and Power Consumption Model}
Here, we define the EH coefficient matrix for the $m$-th element of the $q$-th MM-RIS as $\mathbf{T}_{q,m}=\operatorname{diag} \left( \left[ {0, \dots, 0}, 
1 - \alpha_{q,m}, {0, \dots, 0}\right] \right)$. Therefore, the RF power received by the $m$-th element of the $q$-th MM-RIS is given by $P_{q,m}^{\text{RF}}=\mathbb{E} \left( \left\| \mathbf{T}_{q,m} \left( \mathbf{H}_{q} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} (\mathbf{f}_k^c + \mathbf{f}_k^p)+ \mathbf{n}_{q,m} \right) \right\|^2 \right)$, where $\mathbf{n}_{q,m}$ is the amplified noise introduced by the MM-RIS hardware with power $\sigma_s^2$. To capture the dynamics of the RF energy conversion efficiency for different input power levels, a nonlinear EH model is adopted \cite{14, 31}. Accordingly, the total harvested power of the $m$-th element of the $q$-th MM-RIS is expressed as $P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}} = \frac{\Upsilon_{q,m} - Z\Omega}{1 - \Omega}$, where $\Upsilon_{q,m}=Z / (1 + e^{-\varrho_1 \left( P_{q,m}^{\text{RF}} - \varrho_2 \right)} )$ is a logistic function, and $Z>0$ is a constant determining
the maximum harvested power. Constant $\Omega=\frac{1}{1+e^{\varrho_1 \varrho_2}}$ ensures a zero-input/zero-output response in H mode in conjucation with constants $\varrho_1>0$ and $\varrho_2 > 0$ capturing the joint effects of circuit sensitivity limitations and current leakage. 
 Moreover, the power for controlling the MM-RIS comes from the total number of PIN diodes required for the quantization levels \cite{37n38} of EH ratio, amplitude and phase-shifts defined as $L_{\alpha}$, $L_{\beta}$, and $L_{\theta}$, respectively. Accordingly, the total number of PIN diodes required is given by $\log_2 L_{\alpha} + \log_2 L_{\beta} + 2 \log_2 L_{\theta}$. The effective total power consumption of the $q$-th MM-RIS considers the ME moving stage and communication stage, which is represented by
 \begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{power1}
	P_{q}^{\text{con}}& = 
	\frac{T_{\text{mov}}}{T} \cdot \sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}} v_{q,m} E_{q}^{\text{mov}}
	 + 
	\left(1-\frac{T_{\text{mov}}}{T} \right) \cdot  \left[ \frac{1}{2} \left( \log_{2} L_{\alpha} \right. \right. \notag 
		& \left. \left. + \log_{2} L_{\beta} + 2\log_{2} L_{\theta} \right) \cdot M \cdot P_{\text{pin}} + P_{C} + \xi P_{O,q} \right],
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $P_C$ denotes the power consumed by the RF-to-DC power conversion circuit, and $P_{\text{pin}}$ represents the power consumption per PIN diode. Additionally, $E_{q}^{\text{mov}}$ represents the energy consumption per unit distance due to the movement of MEs. Notation of $\xi$ is the inverse of the amplifier efficiency. The output power of the MM-RIS is given by $P_{O,q} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \left( \sum_{k' \in \mathcal{K}} \|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_q^k \mathbf{H}_q (\mathbf{f}_{k'}^c + \mathbf{f}_{k'}^p) \|^2 + \sigma_s^2 \|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_q^k\|_F^2 \right)$, where $\|\cdot\|_F$ denotes the Frobenius norm. In order to achieve the self-sustainability of each MM-RIS, the total power consumed should not exceed the harvested power by elements, given by $P_{q}^{\text{con}} \leq \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}}$. Therefore, the total power consumption is
\begin{align} \label{power2}
	 P_{\text{tot}} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} (\|\mathbf{f}_{k}^c \|^2 \!+\! \| \mathbf{f}_{k}^p \|^2) + \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}} \left( P^{\text{con}}_q \!-\! \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}} \right),
\end{align}
where the first term indicates the BS beamforming power.
\subsection{Problem Formulation}
The objective is to maximize the system EE while guaranteeing the constraints of minimum user rate requirement, MM-RIS configurations and self-sustainability as well as the operational power limitation, which is formulated as follows:

\begin{subequations} \label{prob}

 \quad \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} \frac{R_{kj}}{P_{\text{tot}}} \label{prob_25a} [4pt]
 \text{s.t.} \quad 
 & \eqref{coupl}, \eqref{con_SIC}, \notag 
 & \mathbf{\Theta}_q \in \mathcal{R}_{\mathbf{\Theta}}, \qquad\forall q \in \mathcal{Q}, \label{prob_25b} [2pt]
 &R_{kj} \geq R^{\text{min}}_{kj}, \qquad \forall j \in \mathcal{J},\, \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \label{prob_25c} 
 & P_{q}^{\text{con}} \leq \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}}, \qquad\qquad \forall q \in \mathcal{Q},  \label{prob_25d} 
 &\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} (\| \mathbf{f}_k^c \|^2+ \| \mathbf{f}_{k}^p \|^2) \leq P_{\text{BS}}^{\text{max}}, \label{prob_25e} 
 &p_{k}^c+\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} p_{kj} = 1, \qquad\ \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \label{prob_25f} 
 & \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} R_{kj}^c \leq \min_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} C_{kj}, \qquad\ \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \label{prob_25g} [2pt]
 &\|\mathbf{r}_{q,m} - \mathbf{r}_{q,m'}\| \geq D, \quad \forall m \neq m', \forall m,m'\in\mathcal{M}, \forall q \in \mathcal{Q}, \label{prob_25h}
 &\mathbf{w}_q \in \mathcal{W}, \qquad \forall q \in \mathcal{Q}. \label{prob_25i}
 \end{align}
\end{subequations}
\endgroup
Constraints \eqref{prob_25b} defines the constraint set of MM-RIS coefficients as $\mathcal{R}_{\mathbf{\Theta}}= \{ \alpha_{q,m} \in \{0,1\}, \beta^k_{q,m} \in [0, \beta^k_{\text{max}}], \theta_{q,m}^k \in [0, 2\pi) | \forall q\in\mathcal{Q}, k\in\mathcal{K}, m\in\mathcal{M} \}$. Constraint \eqref{prob_25c} guarantees the minimum rate requirement of each user as $R_{kj}^{\text{min}}$. Constraint \eqref{prob_25d} ensures the self-sustainability of MM-RIS, i.e., power consumption of the MM-RIS cannot exceed its harvested power. Constraint \eqref{prob_25e} guarantees that transmit power should be smaller than $P^{\text{max}}_{\text{BS}}$. Constraint \eqref{prob_25f} and \eqref{prob_25g} represent the hybrid NOMA-RSMA power allocation factor and rate allocation limitation, respectively. Constraint \eqref{prob_25h} ensures that the distance between two MEs must be greater than the minimum inter-element spacing $D$. Constraint \eqref{prob_25i} defines the deployment boundary of MM-RISs. Due to the non-convexity and non-linearity of the problem, as well as the mixed high-dimensional discrete and continuous variables under highly dynamic environments, solving \eqref{prob} is highly challenging. Hence, we propose an advanced DRL-based approach as detailed in the following section.
\section{Scaling-Law Analysis}
We provide theoretical insights into the scalability of the proposed MM-RIS architecture with respect to the number of MEs $M$. We characterize the scaling behaviors of the desired signal, MM-RIS-induced amplification noise, achievable rate, and EE. Assume that: 1) the element-wise channel coefficients have finite and non-zero first and second moments; 2) the MM-RIS amplification coefficients are bounded as $0\leq \beta_{q,m}^{k} \leq \beta^k_{\text{max}} < \infty$; 3) a non-vanishing fraction of the MM-RIS elements operates in the signal mode as $M$ increases; and 4) the phase-shifts of MM-RISs are configured to coherently combine the desired cascaded channel; 5) the MM-RIS aperture and ME movement velocities are bounded as $M$ increases.
\begin{proposition} \label{prop1}
For each BS-MM-RIS-user cascaded link, under coherent phase configuration, bounded amplification coefficients, and finite channel moments, the desired received signal power scales as $P_{\mathrm{sig}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^2)$, whereas the MM-RIS-induced amplification noise power scales as $P_{\mathrm{AN}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M)$. When the residual interference is bounded, i.e., $P_{\mathrm{I}}(M) = \mathcal{O}(1)$, the SINR reduces to
\begin{align} \label{c1c2}
\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{M^2}{c_1M+c_2} \right) =
\begin{cases}
\mathcal{O}(M^2), & c_1 M \ll c_2, 
\mathcal{O}(M), & c_1 M \gg c_2,
\end{cases}
\end{align}
where $c_1>0$ represents the equivalent MM-RIS amplification noise coefficient, whilst $c_2>0$ collects the receiver noise and disturbance terms. Accordingly, the communication-phase achievable rate satisfies $r(M)=\log_2(1+\gamma(M))
=\mathcal{O}(\log M)$. Under bounded ME movement, the movement time overhead preserves the asymptotic rate scaling, yielding $R(M)=\mathcal{O}(\log M)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The cascaded channel through the $q$-th MM-RIS can be expressed as $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\mathrm{H}} \mathbf{\Theta}_q^{k}\mathbf{H}_q \mathbf{f} = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \alpha_{q,m} \sqrt{\beta_{q,m}^{k}} g_{q,kj,m}^{*} \mathbf{h}_{q,m}^{\rm T} \mathbf{f} e^{j\theta_{q,m}^{k}}$, where $\mathbf{f}$ indicates any beamforming. Under coherent assumption, $\theta_{q,m}^{k}$ compensates for the element-wise phase-shifts of the cascaded channel such that the desired components are coherently combined. Hence, $| \mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\mathrm{H}} \mathbf{\Theta}_q^{k} \mathbf{H}_q \mathbf{f} |  \approx \sum_{m=1}^{M} \alpha_{q,m} \sqrt{\beta_{q,m}^{k}}
|g_{q,kj,m}| |\mathbf h_{q,m}^{\rm T}\mathbf{f} |\triangleq f_1$. Under finite moment assumptions, bounded amplification
coefficients, and a non-vanishing fraction of elements in the signal mode, each element-wise contribution in $f_1$ has a bounded non-zero magnitude. Therefore, the coherently combined amplitude increases linearly with $M$, i.e., $f_1=\mathcal{O}(M)$, which yields $P_{\mathrm{sig}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. On the other hand, the MM-RIS-induced amplification noise associated with the $q$-th MM-RIS is proportional to $\sigma_s^2
\| \mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\rm H} \mathbf{\Theta}_q^{k} \|^2 = \sigma_s^2 \sum_{m=1}^{M} \alpha_{q,m}^{2} \beta_{q,m}^{k} |g_{q,kj,m}|^2$. Since $\beta_{q,m}^{k}$ is bounded and the element-wise channel coefficients have finite moments, each term in the above summation has bounded power. Therefore, the accumulated amplification noise power grows linearly with $M$, yielding $P_{\mathrm{AN}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M)$. Let $P_{\mathrm{I}}(M)$ denote the aggregate residual multi-user interference power after transmit beamforming and hybrid RSMA-NOMA decoding. Combining the desired signal power, residual interference, and total noise terms yields $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{M^2} {P_{\mathrm{I}}(M)+c_1M+c_2} \right)$. When the residual interference is bounded, i.e., $P_{\mathrm I}(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$, we have $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{M^2}{c_1M+c_2} \right)$. When $c_1 M \ll c_2$, the denominator is dominated by the constant, and hence $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}(M^2)$ in \eqref{c1c2}. In contrast, when $c_1 M \gg c_2$, the accumulated MM-RIS amplification noise dominates the denominator, yielding $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}(M)$ in \eqref{c1c2}. Since the communication-stage achievable rate is $r(M)=\log_2\left(1+\gamma(M)\right)$, both $\gamma(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^2)$ and
$\gamma(M)=\mathcal{O}(M)$ lead to $r(M)=\mathcal{O}(\log M)$. According to \eqref{eff_rate}, the effective rate accounting for ME repositioning is $R(M) = \left(1-\frac{T_{\rm mov}(M)}{T}\right)r(M) = \tau(M)r(M)$. Since the MM-RIS movement region is bounded and the ME velocities are lower bounded by a positive constant, $T_{\rm mov}(M)$ remains bounded as $M$ increases, i.e., $\tau(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$. Consequently, $R(M)=\mathcal{O}(\log M)$. This completes the proof.
\end{proof}
\begin{corollary} \label{cor1}
Let the aggregate residual interference scale as $P_{\mathrm I}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{\rho})$, where $ 0\leq \rho \leq 2$, and let the effective total power consumption scale as $P_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{\delta})$, where $0\leq \delta \leq 1$ characterizes the residual element-dependent power overhead after EH. For $\rho < 2$, we have SINR $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( M^{2-\max\{\rho,1\}} \right)$, whereas $\rho=2$ yields an interference-limited regime with $\gamma(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$. Then, the system EE scales as
\begin{align}
\eta_{\mathrm{EE}}(M)
=
\frac{R(M)}{P_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)}
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\mathcal{O}\left(
\frac{\log M}{M^{\delta}}
\right),
& 0\leq\rho<2,[3mm]
\displaystyle
\mathcal{O}\left(
\frac{1}{M^{\delta}}
\right),
& \rho=2.
\end{cases}
\label{EE_scaling}
\end{align}
Hence, when $\delta>0$, the EE asymptotically approaches zero, i.e., $\lim_{M\rightarrow\infty}
\eta_{\mathrm{EE}}(M)=0$.
For the uncompensated element-dependent overhead, i.e., $\delta=1$, the EE scales as $\mathcal{O}(\log M/M)$ for $\rho<2$ and $\mathcal{O}(1/M)$ for $\rho=2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
From Proposition \ref{prop1}, the desired received signal power scales as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$, whereas the MM-RIS-induced amplification noise power scales as $\mathcal{O}(M)$. If the residual interference satisfies
$P_{\mathrm I}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{\rho})$ owing to imperfect interference cancellation, the SINR can be expressed as $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{M^2} {M^{\rho}+M+1} \right)$. For $\rho<2$, the dominant denominator term scales as $\mathcal{O}(M^{\max\{\rho,1\}})$, yielding $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( M^{2-\max\{\rho,1\}} \right)$. Since $2-\max\{\rho,1\}>0$ for $\rho<2$, SINR grows linearly with $M$, and then we have the achievable rate $R(M) = \log_2\left(1+\gamma(M)\right) =\mathcal{O}(\log M)$. When $\rho=2$, the residual interference scales at the same quadratic
order as the desired signal. Hence, $\gamma(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$ provides
$R(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$. According to \eqref{power1} and \eqref{power2}, the effective total power consumption consists of the element-based control, amplification, and movement power after accounting for EH. By characterizing the uncompensated element overhead with the exponent $\delta$, the resulting effective total power can be obtained and scales as $P_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{\delta})$, with $0\leq \delta \leq 1$. Therefore, the EE defined as $\eta_{\mathrm{EE}}(M) = \frac{R(M)}{P_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)}$ scales as \eqref{EE_scaling}. For any $\delta>0$, $M^\delta$ grows asymptotically faster than $\log M$ or any bounded rate term. Therefore, $\eta_{\mathrm{EE}}(M) \rightarrow 0$ as $M \rightarrow \infty$. This completes the proof.
\end{proof}
Proposition \ref{prop1} and Corollary \ref{cor1} reveal the competing effects of coherent array gains, residual interference, amplification noise, and element-based power overhead. Although increasing $M$ provides an $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$ desired signal power gain, the resulting rate grows at most logarithmically when $\rho<2$ and becomes bounded in the interference-limited case of $\rho=2$. Meanwhile, any uncompensated polynomial power growth with $\delta>0$ eventually dominates the rate improvement. Accordingly, increasing the number of MEs does not necessarily improve EE monotonically, and a favorable finite operating region generally exists depending on the balance among array gains, interference, amplification noise, harvested energy, and hardware/movement overhead. This theoretical observation corresponds to the numerical results presented later, where EE initially improves with $M$ but eventually decreases as the additional power overhead outweighs the marginal communication gain.
\section{Proposed CRAFTS Framework}
\label{sec_alg}
\subsection{Multi-Agent Constrained Hybrid DRL}
We consider a multi-agent hybrid DRL framework characterized by state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space $\mathcal{A}$, and reward $\mathcal{R}$. Within this framework as illustrated in Fig. \ref{DRL_plot}, each agent corresponds to either the BS or a single MM-RIS, which interacts with the dynamic environment by taking actions, receiving rewards, and updating its local states accordingly. Conventional centralized DRL methods struggle under conditions of high complexity and slow convergence. Moreover, the use of pure DQN or PPO becomes compellingly impractical, as both quantizing continuous variables into discrete ones and recovering introduce extra overhead and potential quantization errors. To overcome these challenges, we adopt a hybrid DRL architecture that incorporates both DQN and PPO modules for efficiently handling discrete and continuous action spaces. The state, action, and reward are defined as follows:
 \begin{itemize}
 \item \textbf{State:} The total state space is defined as a set of individual agent state $\mathcal{S}(t) = \{s_1(t), s_2(t), \ldots, s_Q(t), s_{Q+1}(t)\}$. Each agent state $s_q(t)$ is designed as $s_q(t) = \{\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}(t) | \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \forall j \in\mathcal{J}_k\}, \forall q\in\mathcal{Q}$ and $s_{Q+1}(t) = \{\mathbf{g}_{kj}(t) | \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \forall j \in\mathcal{J}_k \}$ associated with the combined channel at timestep $t$. We note that index $1\leq q\leq Q$ indicates the MM-RIS agents, whereas $q=Q+1$ stands for the BS agent. The corresponding set of all agents is defined as $\bar{\mathcal{Q}}=\mathcal{Q}\cup \{\text{BS}\}$.
 \item \textbf{Action:} The action space is defined as a set of individual action $ \mathcal{A}(t) = \{ a_1(t), a_2(t), \ldots, a_Q(t), a_{Q+1}(t)\} $. For agents representing MM-RIS $q \in \mathcal{Q}$, each action $a_q(t)= \{ a_q^{\text{dis}}(t), a_q^{\text{con}}(t)\}$ is composed of both discrete and continuous components. Specifically, the discrete action corresponds to the selection of mode of each MM-RIS element, defined as $a_{q}^{\text{dis}}(t) = \{\alpha_{q,m}|\forall m \in \mathcal{M}\}$. On the other hand, the continuous action consists of amplitude, phase-shifts, MM-RIS location, element position, denoted as  $a^{\text{con}}_q(t) = \{ \beta^{k}_{q,m}, \theta^{k}_{q,m}, \mathbf{w}_q, \mathbf{r}_{q,m} | \forall k \in \mathcal{K},  \forall m \in \mathcal{M}\}$. As for the $(Q+1)$-th agent representing the BS, the output action consists of only continuous variables of beamforming, power split factor and common rate allocation, denoted as $a_{Q+1}(t) = \{ \mathbf{f}_{k}^c, \mathbf{f}_{k}^p, p_{k}^c, p_{kj}, R_{kj}^c  | \forall k\in\mathcal{K}, j\in\mathcal{J}_k\}$.
 
 \item \textbf{Reward:} 
The instantaneous shared reward is attained as the overall EE in conjunction with its constraints, given by
\begin{align} \label{rew}
	r(t) = \sum_{k\in \mathcal{K}}\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} \frac{R_{kj}}{P_{\text{total}}}, \quad \text{ s.t. }  \eqref{prob_25b} \text{-} \eqref{prob_25i}.
\end{align}
Note that all agents share the reward feedback by the environments, i.e., $r_q(t)=r(t)$ for all $q\in\bar{\mathcal{Q}}$.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Lagrangian-based Constrained DRL}
Most existing works adopt penalty-based reward designs \cite{han}; however, tuning the associated penalty coefficients is often labor-intensive and highly sensitive to system configurations. Furthermore, employing hierarchical RL or metaheuristic approaches \cite{my_rl_yt} to optimize the hyperparameters of the primary RL framework may introduce excessive computational and training overhead. These methods also do not guarantee the satisfaction of constraints. Therefore, inspired by \cite{35}, we propose a Lagrangian-based method to iteratively guarantee the satisfaction of all involved constraints. The shared reward can be designed using the augmented Lagrangian in conjunction with the constraints as penalties, given by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{rew_lag}
	\mathcal{L}_{\text{aug}}(\Xi, \boldsymbol{\nu},\boldsymbol{\mu}) &= \mathbbm{E} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r(t) \right]  \!-\! \sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}} \sum_{\ell\in \mathcal{C}} \nu_{q,\ell}  \mathcal{C}_{q,\ell} \!-\! \upsilon  \mathcal{H},
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $\gamma^t\in[0,1]$ is the discount factor at episode $t$ indicating the importance of future rewards. $\mathcal{C}$ indicates the set of inequality constraints, whilst $\Xi$ means the policy of DRL. Notations of $\nu_{q,\ell}$ and $\upsilon$ are Lagrangian multipliers standing for the penalty coefficients for inequality constraints $\mathcal{C}_{q,\ell}$ and equality constraint $\mathcal{H}$, respectively. The constraint penalties are given by
$\mathcal{C}_{q,1} = \sum_{m\in \mathcal{M}} \left[ \frac{1 - (\beta_{q,m}^{\rm r})^2 - (\beta_{q,m}^{\rm t})^2}{2} - \beta_{q,m}^{\rm r} \beta_{q,m}^{\rm t} \cos(\theta_{q,m}^{\rm t} - \theta_{q,m}^{\rm r}) \right]$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,2} =  \sum_{m\in \mathcal{M}} \left[ \beta_{q,m}^{\rm r} \beta_{q,m}^{\rm t} \cos(\theta_{q,m}^{\rm t} - \theta_{q,m}^{\rm r}) - \frac{(\beta_{q,m}^{\rm r})^2 + (\beta_{q,m}^{\rm t})^2 - 1}{2} \right]$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,3} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_k} \sum_{l\in\mathcal{L}_{kj}\setminus j} \left( \gamma_{kj\rightarrow kj}^{p} - \gamma_{kl\rightarrow kj}^{p} \right)$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,4} = \sum_{k\in \mathcal{K}}  \sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} \left( R^{\text{min}}_{kj} - R_{kj} \right)$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,5} = P_{q}^{\text{con}} - \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}}$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,6} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} (\| \mathbf{f}_k^c \|^2+ \| \mathbf{f}_{k}^p \|^2) - P_{\text{BS}}^{\text{max}}$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,7} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \left( \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} R_{kj}^c - \min_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} C_{kj} \right)$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,8} =  \sum_{\substack{m,m'\in \mathcal{M},  m\neq m'}} \left( D - \|\mathbf{r}_{q,m} - \mathbf{r}_{q,m'}\| \right)$
,
and
$\mathcal{H} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \left( p_{k}^c+\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} p_{kj} - 1 \right)$. 
To solve the constrained DRL problem in \eqref{rew_lag}, we employ a Lagrangian relaxation-based approach \cite{42, 43} to enable agents to learn a constraint-aware policy by balancing the trade-off between network performance and operational safety. The corresponding Lagrangian primal-dual problem is derived by
\begin{align}
 \min_{\nu_{q,\ell} \geq 0, \upsilon \geq 0} \max_{\Xi} \ \mathcal{L}_{\text{aug}}(\Xi, \boldsymbol{\nu},\boldsymbol{\upsilon})
 \label{lagr}.
\end{align}
In order to solve the min-max problem in \eqref{lagr}, we adopt an alternative optimization iteratively obtaining the primal-dual solutions. That is, for each iteration, the policy $\Xi$ served as primal variables and the dual variables of $\{ \nu_{q,\ell},\upsilon \}$ tackling constraints are updated alternately. Thus, after conducting the main DRL scheme of policy $\Xi$, the dual variables can be updated by minimizing the dual subproblem of
\begin{align}
 \min_{\nu_{q,\ell} \geq 0, \upsilon \geq 0} \  \sum_{\ell\in \mathcal{C}} \nu_{q,\ell} \cdot \mathcal{C}_{q,\ell} + \upsilon \cdot \mathcal{H}.
\end{align}
The dual variables are then updated to minimize violations by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{d_update}
	\nu_{q, \ell} \leftarrow \left[ \nu_{q, \ell} + b_{q,\ell} \cdot \mathcal{C}_{q,\ell}\right]^{+}, \qquad 
	\upsilon \leftarrow \left[\upsilon + b_{\upsilon} \cdot \mathcal{H} \right]^{+},
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $\{b_{q,\ell}, b_{\upsilon}\}$ indicate the learning rates of dual variables, whilst $[\cdot]^{+}$ denotes the projection onto the non-negative orthant. Different from the conventional Lagrangian methods where dual learning rates are fixed, the proposed framework adopts a joint action-multiplier optimization mechanism. The corresponding Lagrangian-based action is defined as $a_{q}^{\text{aug}}(t) = \{b_{q,\ell}, b_{\upsilon} | \ell \in\mathcal{C} \}$ for each agent $q \in \bar{\mathcal{Q}}$. Since all multipliers are continuous, the new action is presented as $\bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}(t) = \{ a^{\text{con}}_q(t), a_{q}^{\text{aug}}(t)\}$.
\subsubsection{MADQN for Discrete Policy}
MADQN employs a deep neural network, termed Q-network, to approximate the Q-function $Q_q(s_q(t), a_q^{\text{dis}}(t)| \omega_q^{\phi})$ which estimates the expected cumulative reward for each action $a_q^{\text{dis}}(t)$ under a given state $s_q(t)$. Note that we define $\omega^{\phi}_q$ and $\omega^{\phi^{-}}_q$ as the model weights of the current network and of the target network of DQN, respectively. Based on the estimated Q-value, each agent selects its action using an $\epsilon$-greedy strategy, which balances exploration and exploitation by choosing a random action with probability $\epsilon(t)$ and by selecting the action with the maximum predicted Q-value with probability $ 1 - \epsilon(t)$. We design the decaying exploration as $\epsilon(t) =\epsilon(t-1) - \frac{\epsilon_{\text{max}} - \epsilon_{\text{min}}}{\epsilon_d}$, where $\epsilon_d$ is the decaying constant. Notations of $\epsilon_{\text{max}}$ and $\epsilon_{\text{min}}$ indicate the maximum and minimum exploration rates, respectively. To enhance training stability, MADQN incorporates two critical techniques \cite{38}: 
(i)
\textit{Experience replay buffer} stores historical trajectories with a tuple of $ (s_q(t), a_q^{\text{dis}}(t), r_q(t), s_q(t+1))$, which allows the agent to sample mini-batches uniformly and eliminate temporal correlations during learning, where $s_q(t+1)$ indicates the newly observed state;
(ii) 
\textit{Target network update} is developed with its model denoted as $Q'_q(s_q(t), a_q^{\text{dis}}(t)| \omega_q^{\phi^-})$, which is periodically softly updated to provide stable DRL learning, i.e., $\omega_q^{\phi^-} \leftarrow \tau_{\phi} \cdot \omega_q^{\phi} + ( 1 - \tau_{\phi})  \cdot \omega_q^{\phi^-}$ where $\tau_{\phi}$ indicates the importance of target model of MADQN. The Q-network is then updated by minimizing the temporal-difference error, which measures the discrepancy between the predicted and the target Q-values, which is represented by 
$\mathcal{L}(\omega_{q}^\phi) = 
\mathbb{E}
\left\lbrace
\left[
y_q - Q_{q} (s_{q}(t), a_{q}^{\text{dis}}(t) | \omega_{q}^\phi)
\right]^{2}
\right\rbrace$,
where $y_q = r_q(t) + \gamma^{\text{dis}} \cdot \max_{a'} Q'_{q} (s_{q}(t+1), a' | \omega_{q}^{\phi^-})$ indicates the temporal difference target value and the discount factor $\gamma^d \in [0, 1] $ means the importance of future rewards.
Note that $r_q(t)=r(t), \forall q\in\mathcal{Q}$ is derived from \eqref{rew_lag} containing penalty constraints. Notation of $Q'_q(\cdot)$ is the Q-value of the target network of agent $q$. The parameter update via gradient descent is expressed as $\omega_{q}^\phi \leftarrow \omega_{q}^\phi - \eta^{\text{dis}} \cdot \nabla_{\omega_{q}^\phi} \, \mathcal{L}(\omega_{q}^\phi)$, where $\eta^{\text{dis}} \in [0, 1] $ presents the learning rate of MADQN.
\subsubsection{MAPPO for Continuous Policy}
The remaining continuous parameters are optimized using the PPO algorithm \cite{39}. Particularly, MAPPO adopts an actor-critic framework in a multi-agent manner, where each agent consisting of a policy network for actor and of a value network for critic. In the policy network, the neural network outputs the mean and standard deviation of a multivariate Gaussian distribution, where actions are sampled according to the current state $s_q(t)$ and policy $\pi_{\delta_q}(\bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}(t)|s_q(t))$. Note that $\delta_q$ indicates the policy network parameters. To optimize the policy network, we employ a clipped surrogate objective function which is given by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{loss_clip}
	\mathcal{L}^{\text{clip}} (\delta_q) 
= - {\mathbb{E}}_t & \big[ \min\big( O_q(\delta_q)\hat{A}_q(t), \notag 
&\quad \mathrm{clip}( O_q(\delta_q), 1 - \Lambda, 1 + \Lambda)\hat{A}_q(t) \big) \big], 
\end{align} 
\endgroup
where ${\mathbb{E}}[\cdot]$ is the expectation over a batch of generated trajectories, and $O_q(\delta_q) = \frac{\pi_{\delta_q}(\bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}(t)|s_q(t))}{\pi_{\delta_{q,\text{old}}}(\bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}(t)|s_q(t))}$ is the probability ratio. $\mathrm{clip}(\cdot)$ indicates the clipping function which clips the change between the new and old policies within a range of $[1-\Lambda, 1+\Lambda]$ to avoid excessive policy updates. Note that $\delta_{q,\text{old}}(\cdot)$ indicates the old policy parameters. Furthermore, $\hat{A}_q(t)$ is the generalized advantage estimation (GAE) quantifying the difference between the observed outcome of each action in a state and the predicted state value $ V_{\mu_q}(s_q(t))$ by the value network, represented by
$\hat{A}_q(t) = \sum_{i=t}^{T_{\text{tr}}-t}(\gamma^{\text{con}} \lambda^{\text{con}})^{i-t} \cdot \left\lbrace [ (r(i) + \gamma^{\text{con}} V_{\mu_q} (s_q(i+1)) ] - V_{\mu_q} (s_q(i)) \right\rbrace$, where $\gamma^{\text{con}}$ and $\lambda^{\text{con}}$ indicate the importance ratio and GAE hyperparameters of MAPPO, respectively. Notation $T_{\text{tr}}$ means the length of trajectory segment. Note that $r(i)$ follows \eqref{rew_lag} containing penalty constraints. The policy is optimized iteratively by maximizing the clipped surrogate objective using gradient ascent given by $\delta_q \leftarrow {\delta_q} - \eta^{\text{con}}_{\text{a}} \cdot \nabla_{\delta_q} \mathcal{L}^{\text{clip}} (\delta_q)$, where $\eta^{\text{con}}_{\text{a}} \in [0, 1] $ represents the learning rate of the actor in MAPPO. The associated loss function of the value network is defined as 
\begin{align} \label{loss_value}
	\mathcal{L}^{V}(\mu_q) = \mathbb{E}_t [  \big( V_{\mu_q}(s_q(t)) - \hat{V}^{\text{tar}}_q(t) \big)^2],
\end{align}
where $\hat{V}^{\text{tar}}_q(t) 
= V_{\mu_q^-}\!\big(s_q(t)\big) + \hat{A}_q(t)$ and $\mu_q^-$ indicates the previous update of the value network. The parameters of value network are updated by the gradient method, i.e., $\mu_q \leftarrow {\mu_q} - \eta^{\text{con}}_{\text{c}} \cdot \nabla_{\mu_q} \mathcal{L}^{V} (\mu_q)$, where $\eta^{\text{con}}_{\text{c}} \in [0, 1] $ is learning rate for critic in MAPPO.
\subsection{Intra-Agent Bi-Directional Parametrized Sharing}
\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=3in]{fig/agm3.eps}
\caption{The proposed bi-directional parametrized sharing and federated transformer architecture for intra-agent and inter-agent coordination, respectively.} 
\label{interintra}
\end{figure}
In the context of individual agent design in hybrid DRL, PPO and DQN typically select actions independently based on their respective input states. This isolated decision-making process neglects the potential interdependence and interaction between the two strategies within intra-agent structure. To address this, inspired by the single-directional sharing mechanism in \cite{my_ps, 30, 31}, we propose a bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanism as depicted at bottom of Fig. \ref{DRL_plot}, where the details are illustrated in Fig. \ref{interintra}. The core idea is to enable the shared representation between the PPO and DQN models by exchanging features. Specifically, PPO agent utilizes the discrete action output from the DQN agent as the input of PPO, i.e., $s_q^{\text{con}}(t) = \operatorname{concat} ( s_q(t), \operatorname{vec}(a_q^{\text{dis}}(t-1)) )$, where ${\rm concat}(\cdot)$ indicates the concatenation of two vectors and ${\rm vec}(\cdot)$ vectorizes the action. Similarly, DQN agent also employ the continuous action output from PPO as the input, derived by $s_q^{\text{dis}}(t) = \operatorname{concat} ( s_q(t), \operatorname{vec}(a_q^{\text{con}}(t-1)) )$. 
Note that the parametrized sharing is only applied to the MM-RIS agents due to their hybrid discrete-continuous action structures, which improves the coordination between the two decision-making modules.
\subsection{Inter-Agent Federated Transformer} 
Considering all state features with equal importance is impractical in MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA systems since different channel conditions and communication variables may contribute unequally to the decision-making process. Therefore, we incorporate a transformer-based mechanism \cite{32, my_ojcom} to adaptively assign distinct importance weights to different state features, as depicted at top-left of Fig. \ref{DRL_plot}. Accordingly, instead of directly utilizing the raw observation state, each agent first processes the state through a multi-head self-attention architecture associated with the linearly projected \textit{query}, \textit{key}, and \textit{value}, given by $Y_{\text{qu}} = W_{\text{qu}} s_{q}(t),
Y_{\text{ke}} = W_{\text{ke}} s_{q}(t),
Y_{\text{va}} = W_{\text{va}} s_{q}(t),$
where $W_{\text{qu}/\text{ke}/\text{va}}$ denote trainable projection matrices. Subsequently, the attention output is computed through the scaled dot-product operation as
\begin{align}\label{att}
B = \mathrm{Att}(Y_{\text{qu}}, Y_{\text{ke}}, Y_{\text{va}}) = \mathrm{Softmax} \left( \frac{Y_{\text{qu}} Y_{\text{ke}}^{\mathrm{T}}}{\sqrt{d_{\text{ke}}}} \right) \cdot Y_{\text{va}},
\end{align}
where $\mathrm{Att}(\cdot)$ denotes the attention operation and $\mathrm{Softmax}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{x_j}}$ represents the softmax activation function. The notation $d_{\text{ke}}$ indicates the feature dimension of the key space associated with $W_{\text{ke}}$. 
To further improve feature extraction capability and avoid the limitation of relying on a single attention representation, a multi-head attention structure is incorporated. Specifically, the transformed attention-aware state is generated by concatenating multiple attention heads, expressed as $s'_{q}(t) \!=\! \mathrm{MH}(Y_{\text{qu}}, Y_{\text{ke}}, Y_{\text{va}}) \!=\! \operatorname{concat}(B_1, B_2, ..., B_{N_{\text{he}}}) W_{\text{out}}$,
where $\mathrm{MH}(\cdot)$ denotes the multi-head attention operation, and $B_{n_{\text{he}}} = \mathrm{Att}(\cdot)$ is the attention output corresponding to the $n_{\text{he}}$-th attention head obtained from \eqref{att}. Moreover, $N_{\text{he}}$ denotes the number of attention heads, whereas $W_{\text{out}}$ is the trainable output projection matrix.
While the parametrized sharing mechanism effectively facilitates the coordination between MAPPO and MADQN within intra-agent, the lack of information exchanged between agents potentially leads to suboptimal solutions. To address the challenge, we design a decentralized coordination scheme by incorporating FL into the multi-agent system \cite{34, 41}, as shown at right of Fig. \ref{DRL_plot}, where the details are depicted in Fig. \ref{interintra}. Particularly, each agent independently maintains local DQN and PPO modules for distributed action execution. The local model parameters are then periodically uploaded to an aggregation server, which can be implemented at the edge or BS controller. Considering the distinct learning characteristics of continuous and discrete policies, the edge performs decoupled model aggregation for the PPO and DQN modules separately. The aggregation global model updates for round $t+1$ are expressed as
\begin{align} \label{fl_agg}
\omega_{\text{glo}} = 
\begin{cases}
	\frac{1}{Q} \sum_{q \in 
	\mathcal{Q}} \varsigma_q \cdot \omega_{q}, \qquad \text{if } \omega_{q}= \omega_{q}^{\phi}, 
	\frac{1}{Q+1} \sum_{q \in \bar{\mathcal{Q}}} \varsigma_q \cdot \omega_{q}, \quad \text{if } \omega_{q}\in\{ \delta_q, \mu_q \},
\end{cases}
\end{align}
where $\varsigma_q \in [0, 1]$ represents the importance weight of agent $q$. It is worth noticing that $\omega_q$ consists of transformer-related trainable model weights of $W_{\text{qu}/\text{ke}/\text{va}/\text{out}}$ per agent. This parallel aggregation process ensures global policy consistency across distributed agents while preserving local data privacy and reducing communication overhead. After the decoupled aggregation, the updated global parameters are broadcast to all local agents, i.e., $\omega_{q} \leftarrow \omega_{\text{glo}}$ for subsequent training and policy refinement.
\begin{algorithm}[!t]
\caption{Proposed CRAFTS Scheme}
\footnotesize
\label{alg}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\STATE \textbf{Initialization:}
\STATE \quad 1) Initialize environment and MADQN/MAPPO networks
\STATE \quad 2) Initialize transformer parameters and set
$a_{q}^{\text{dis}}, \bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}$, $\forall q\in\bar{\mathcal Q}$
\STATE \quad 3) Initialize Lagrangian multipliers $\nu_{q,\ell}$ and $\upsilon$
\STATE \quad 4) Initialize replay buffer $\mathcal{D}_{q}$ and trajectory/mini-batch set $\mathcal{X}_{q}$
\FOR{$t = 1$ to $T$}

 \IF{$q \in \mathcal{Q}$}
 \STATE $a^{\text{dis}}_{q}(t) \leftarrow {\rm MADQN} ( {\rm concat}(s'_{q}(t), a^{\text{con}}_{q}(t-1)) )$
 \STATE $\bar{a}^{\text{con}}_{q}(t) \leftarrow {\rm MAPPO} ( {\rm concat}(s'_{q}(t),a^{\text{dis}}_{q}(t-1)) )$
 \ELSE
 \STATE $\bar{a}^{\text{con}}_{q}(t) \leftarrow {\rm MAPPO}(s'_{q}(t))$
 \ENDIF

 \ENDFOR
 \FOR{$q \in \bar{\mathcal{Q}}$}
 \STATE Observe $s_{q}(t+1)$ and obtain shared reward $r_{q}(t)=r(t)$
 \STATE Store transition/trajectory samples in $\mathcal{D}_{q}$ and $\mathcal{X}_{q}$
 \STATE \textbf{(MADQN Module):}
 \IF{$q \in \mathcal{Q}$}

 \STATE Perform gradient descent to update $\omega^{\phi}_{q}$
 \STATE Soft update target MADQN parameters
 \ENDIF

 \STATE Compute GAE $\hat{A}_{q}(t)$ and target value

 \STATE \textbf{(Lagrangian Update):}
 \STATE Update $\nu_{q,\ell}$ and $\upsilon$ according to \eqref{d_update} using $a^{\text{aug}}_{q}(t)$
 \ENDFOR

 \ENDIF

The overall procedure of the proposed CRAFTS scheme is summarized in Algorithm \ref{alg}. The process begins by initializing the MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA environment, the local MADQN and MAPPO networks, the transformer modules, and the Lagrangian multipliers for all agents. At each time step, the local state of each agent is first processed by the transformer-based feature extractor. For each MM-RIS and BS agent, the discrete and continuous actions are then jointly determined by MADQN and MAPPO, respectively, where the bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanism exchanges the previous continuous and discrete actions between the two policy branches. In addition, MAPPO determines the continuous Lagrangian-related actions for adaptively updating the dual variables. The resulting joint actions are executed in the environment, after which the agents observe the updated states and obtain the shared reward. Subsequently, the MADQN and MAPPO parameters are updated according to their respective learning procedures, followed by the primal-dual updates of the Lagrangian multipliers. Moreover, the local model parameters are periodically aggregated through the FL mechanism and the updated global parameters are broadcast back to the agents. The above procedure is repeated until the prescribed training horizon is reached.

Among the benchmarks, DQN achieves the lowest EE performance since its discrete-action structure suffers from the curse of dimensionality and lacks the capability to efficiently optimize high-dimensional continuous communication variables. Meanwhile, CRAFTS-FT integrating FL and transformer achieves superior stability and higher EE compared to benchmarks. \subsection{Effect of MF-RIS Elements}
